title: Strunk's Elements of Style
note: William Strunk Jr., who taught English at Cornell, wrote The Elements of Style as a short handbook of rules for plain English; the 1918 text is in the public domain. His student E. B. White later revised and expanded it. Quotations here follow the Project Gutenberg text exactly.

read.title: A little book of rules
text: William Strunk Jr. wrote The Elements of Style for his English students, and its opening line states its aim: "This book aims to give in brief space the principal requirements of plain English style." The book is famous for its short, commanding rules.

Some rules govern usage and punctuation. Rule 5 reads "Do not join independent clauses by a comma," which is the ban on the comma splice. Rule 7 reads "A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject," which is the rule against dangling modifiers.
Others govern composition. "Use the active voice." "Put statements in positive form." "Use definite, specific, concrete language." And the most quoted of all: "Omit needless words."

Strunk was less rigid than his reputation. He wrote that the active voice is usually more direct, but that a writer should not entirely discard "the passive voice, which is frequently convenient and sometimes necessary." And his case for concision was not a demand for short sentences. What he asked was that the writer "make every word tell."
Read this way, the book is less a list of laws than a set of strong defaults: start from them, and break one only when you know why.

q.q: Which Strunk rule forbids the comma splice?
o: Do not join independent clauses by a comma.

q.q: What did Strunk say about the passive voice?
o: It is always weaker than the active
